title: Runtime fragmentation: latency & cost digest
content:
Executive summary:
This note documents a focused bench to quantify the effects of runtime fragmentation (inefficient GPU slot utilization caused by heterogenous sequence lengths, small batch arrivals, and preemptive slot losses) on 1) median/tail latency and 2) dollars-per-1k-token. It is exploratory and intentionally lightweight — goal is to surface magnitude and dominant modes so product/serving can prioritize mitigations.

Key findings (high level):
- Fragmentation increases p95 latency by ~18–42% depending on workload mix; worst cases occur at low concurrency with high variance in request length.
- Cost per 1k tokens (amortized on reserved capacity) increases by 6–22% when fragmentation prevents optimal tiling/packing.
- Simple slot-repacking heuristics (greedy length-sorted packing, 30s micro-batch hold) recover ~60–80% of the lost cost efficiency with modest p99 impact.

Experiment setup:
- Model: stable-xxl-8b (quantized int8 preset ql2) — representative open model in catalog.
- HW: Dedicated A100-simulated pool (8 GPU nodes), pricing assumptions = committed reserved capacity monthly amortized cost per node.
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes generated from production trace samples:
  * steady-chat (low variance, mean tokens 120, 95th 210)
  * conversational-mixed (median 64, long-tail to 2048 ~0.8%)
  * ad-hoc-long (large variance, median 40, heavy tail 4096 tokens ~2.5%)
- Strategies compared:
  1) baseline immediate-schedule (no hold, first-fit slot allocation)
  2) eager-batch (30ms aggregation window)
  3) micro-hold (30s micro-batch hold to aggregate session requests when slots free)
  4) length-sorted-packing (greedy pack by descending seq length)
  5) hybrid (length-sorted + 300ms light hold)
- Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms), tokens served per GPU-hour, dollars per 1k tokens (approx), slot occupancy fraction, fragmentation index (see below).

Fragmentation index (simple):
  fragmentation_index = 1 - (sum(active_token_capacity_used) / sum(slot_capacity_allocated))
  - Expresses fraction of allocated token capacity left unused due to mismatched packing.

Results (numbers aggregated across 72h runs):
- Table (text):
  Workload | Strategy | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | token/hr/GPU | $/1k tokens | frag_idx
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  steady-chat | baseline | 120 | 310 | 72k | $0.83 | 0.12
  steady-chat | length-sort | 98 | 295 | 86k | $0.70 | 0.06
  conversational-mixed | baseline | 210 | 540 | 61k | $0.98 | 0.19
  conversational-mixed | micro-hold | 190 | 560 | 75k | $0.81 | 0.10
  ad-hoc-long | baseline | 330 | 890 | 49k | $1.12 | 0.22
  ad-hoc-long | hybrid | 285 | 950 | 62k | $0.92 | 0.11

Text charts (ASCII-style):
- Cost delta vs baseline ($/1k tokens):
  baseline: [##########] $1.00 (normalized)
  length-sort: [#######   ] $0.83 (-17%)
  micro-hold:   [########  ] $0.88 (-12%)
  hybrid:       [######    ] $0.78 (-22%)

- p95 latency improvement over baseline (lower better):
  steady-chat: baseline=120ms | length-sort=98ms  (≈18% better)
    bars: baseline: |||||||||||| (120)  length-sort: ||||||||| (98)
  ad-hoc-long: baseline=330ms | hybrid=285ms (≈14% better)
    bars: baseline: ||||||||||||||||||| (330) hybrid: |||||||||||||||| (285)

Observations and interpretation:
- Low-concurrency, high-variance traffic is the worst case for fragmentation because slots are partially filled often and preemption/evictions amplify unused capacity.
- Length-sorted greedy packing is cheap to implement in the router and recovers most of the efficiency for steady and mixed workloads, with negligible p95 regressions in those mixes.
- Micro-hold strategies recover tokens-per-hour by waiting for compatible requests to arrive, but introduce a latency tail risk; optimal hold windows depend on SLA (30ms–300ms range looked best in our sims).
- Hybrid (sort+short-hold) gives the best cost/lambda trade-off: about ~60–80% recovery of ideal packing with small p95 increases; p99 needs careful instrumentation because long-tail blocking events can still add high-latency outliers.

Failure modes and caveats:
- These tests assume permissive routing (we can reorder small requests). For strict FIFO ordering (session consistency), packing gains shrink by ~40%.
- Quantization profile changes: moving from ql2->ql3 shifted token/hr/GPU down ~6% (more compute), which interacts multiplicatively with fragmentation — when compute bound, packing gains are smaller.
- Our dollar numbers are amortized on reserved capacity; burst-on-demand pricing will amplify absolute $/1k but relative percentages remain similar.

Actionable recommendations (short-term):
1) Implement a length-sorted packing mode in the router as opt-in for dedicated pools (low-dev cost; significant upside).
2) Add a micro-hold feature behind a flag with configurable windows per SLO tier (start 50ms default for non-interactive tiers).
3) Instrument fragmentation_index and expose per-tenant metric in Console (tag by route/model/quant-profile) so Optimize can recommend packing policies.
4) Run production canary on 5% of Dedicated traffic for 2 weeks to measure p99 impact before broad rollout.

Longer-term ideas:
- Slot-cost-aware preemption: prefer preempting slots with lower expected leftover capacity to reduce fragmentation when reclaiming capacity.
- Adaptive hold windows based on recent arrival rates and session-stickiness signals.
- Combine with KV-cache locality: co-locate sequences likely to share KV cache to avoid cache misses when packing distinct sessions.

Open questions / research tasks:
- What is user-visible latency perception vs p95/p99 for interactive UIs? we need UX experiments.
- For multi-tenant mixed workloads, what is fair scheduling policy that balances cost-efficiency and latency fairness?
- How does fragmentation interact with multi-model packing (different architectures)? preliminary tests show non-linear effects; schedule an architecture compatibility sweep.
